messages.subject: Re: which variables, and how many, to match on?
messages.subject_clean: which variables, and how many, to match on?
messages.body_plain:
Hi--
I would add two more considerations--the more covariates then your 
predictive model become better and better (presumably), driving the 
distribution of propensity scores apart.  Perfect prediction also 
becomes more common as well.   If this happens, one can view this in one 
of two ways.  First, you'll have fewer cases for which you can estimate 
the treatment effect.  Second, I guess it's better to know that the 
groups actually do differ on these characteristics

The other issue is that once you start doing checks for balance, you'll 
get more and more between-group differences by chance alone--one can get 
get caught in a bit of an infinite loop, checking  balance, fixing what 
you find, checking again and so on.

regards,
michael

Gary King wrote:
>
> I'd add that, unlike controlling for variables in linear regression or 
> other parametric techniques, including variables that are more highly 
> collinear with each other in matching will not explode your standard 
> errors and make your analysis less efficient.  So some of the 40 vars 
> you have might all be pretty closely related, in which case its like 
> controlling for just one or a few.
>
> Also, if you intend to run a parametric analysis after matching, as we 
> recommend, and you have a list of variables you intend to include in 
> that analysis, you should probably match on all those variables prior 
> to the parametric analysis.  If you don't, then you're controlling via 
> the assumptions of your model.  if there aren't enough observations 
> after matching on all those variables, then you may be stuck with the 
> controlling via the model.
>
> Gary
>
> On Wed, 31 Oct 2007, Elizabeth Stuart wrote:
>
>> Hi Casey,
>> Here are my thoughts on this issue.  It is a matter of some debate in 
>> the
>> matching literature, though, so others may have other ideas.
>>
>> 1.  Match on as many variables as you, and certainly check the 
>> balance on
>> all of the ones you have observed, even if you don't actually match 
>> on them.
>> This can be done in MatchIt using the "addlvariables" option in the
>> summary() command.
>>
>> 2.  If you have enough observations, you should be able to match on 
>> all 40
>> variables.
>>
>> 3.  People generally stay away from selecting the variables to 
>> include based
>> on analyses of the outcome data in their dataset, to avoid modeling the
>> outcome (or even analyzing the outcome) before finishing the matching.
>> Instead, the selection is usually based on which variables are a priori
>> believed to affect both treatment assignment and the outcome (true
>> confounders).  Some research has shown that it is better to be 
>> inclusive in
>> the matching, in that it is better to include irrelevant variables 
>> than it
>> is to exclude relevant ones, but again, this is a topic of recent 
>> research
>> and some recent simulations have shown that including variables that are
>> independent of the outcome can be inefficient.
>>
>> 4.  In situations I have been in where we had more variables than we 
>> really
>> could match on, I have made a priority list of the variables on which 
>> it was
>> particularly important to get good balance (e.g., pre-treatment 
>> measures of
>> the outcome variables of interest or other variables I believe are 
>> highly
>> predictive of the outcome).  Then fit a propensity score model with 
>> those
>> important ones, and check the balance on all of the variables.  If 
>> there are
>> some other variables that are badly balanced in the resulting matched 
>> data,
>> include them in a second iteration of the propensity score. Iterate 
>> until
>> you get good balance overall.
>>
>> I hope this helps,
>> Liz
>>
>> On 10/30/07 1:06 PM, "Casey Klofstad" <klofstad-Re5JQEeQqe8AvxtiuMwx3w at public.gmane.org> wrote:
>>
>>> Hey all-
>>>
>>> I have the fortune of having around 40 pre-treatment variables that I
>>> can match on. Should I use them all?
>>>
>>> If not, is there a systematic way to choose which variables to
>>> include? For example, should I just use the ones that correlate the
>>> most with the treatment and the outcome?
>>>
>>> Thanks!

messages.subject: am I ready for analysis?
messages.body_plain:
I'm wondering whether I am ready to proceed to analysis:

(1) I ran optimal matching. The original N was 1044. The matched N =
996 (498 treated and 498 control).

(2) I took a "naive" approach by putting all of the 109 pre-treatment
variables I had on hand into the matching model. A handful of the
variables I dumped in have a standardized difference > .2 in the
matched data set (x = 8), but this is better than in the original data
(x = 12).

(3) One additional thing I did notice is that the distance measure is
not very well matched (std. diff. = .8), but it is improved from the
unmated data set (std. diff = 1.0).

Thanks,

-c

-- 
Casey A. Klofstad

Department of Political Science
Coral Gables, FL

messages.subject: Re: am I ready for analysis?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Casey,
Without having seen all the output and not knowing more than what you say
below, I would play around with the matching a bit more.

>From my read below, you start out with 498 treated and 546 control, and do
1:1 matching to get 498 treated and 498 control.  That doesn't leave many
controls not matched, so the matching really isn't doing much--that's
probably why your balance doesn't look much better after matching as
compared to before.  (Matching works best with at least twice as many
controls as treated--at an extreme, if you start out with the same # of
treated and control the matching won't do anything!).  If I were you I would
look into subclassification or full matching, to see if they work better
given your data structure.


Hopefully doing some other approach will help, but in terms of the # of
variables with standardized differences > .2, I would also look at which
ones are problematic before and after--are they ones you believe are
particularly related to the outcome of interest?  If so you might want to do
something special for them, e.g., exact or Mahalanobis matching.

Liz

perhaps it's a reflection of the things I study but I always start with 
a couple of things to improve balance
Namely , I run completely separate propensity score models by gender and 
by race/ethnicity.  That often seems to help quite a bit.
generally speaking, pooling models of developmental outcomes across boys 
and girls is a bad idea. 

(It didn't help in a recent analysis of data from an evaluation of a 
mental health intervention.  In that instance, running separate models 
by gender or by race/ethnicity did virtually nothing.  I was surprised.  
What did make a big difference was when I chopped the sample up by broad 
diagnostic categories and ran separate models.  That did the trick.  You 
could do the same thing with a bunch of interactions.)

regards,
michael foster

messages.subject: which Stata weight to use?
messages.body_plain:
I have matched data via full matching, and I want to analyze the data
in Stata. I know I need to use a regression weight becuase I have
subclasses, but which one is the appropriate one?

Specifically, Stata offers three potential choices: pweights,
aweights, and iweights

For the record, I get the same results with "a" and "i". The "p"
weight slightly alters the results (becuase it switches over to robust
standard errors).

Also, I setx/estsimp in Clarify will not take "i" and "p" weight
estimates. In these cases Clarify will estimate and aggregate the
model results, but it will not calculate predicted probabilities or
expected values. Clarify has no problem with "a" weights.

Thanks!

-- 
Casey A. Klofstad
University of Miami
Department of Political Science
Coral Gables, FL

messages.subject: Re: which Stata weight to use?
messages.body_plain:
Well, I don't know what -clarify- does, but to me it seems like the 
bigger question is how to use the weights. 
(Most likely, the weights are a feature of your data, and you have 
-pweights-.)

At the matching stage, I would use the weight as a covariate for 
calculating the propensity score.  If your weights are a function of 
covariates already in the model, I wouldn't expect much of an impact.

At the analysis stage, you might think of using weights when calculating 
the mean treatment difference by pooling across strata or levels of the 
propensity score. 
I can't see where the weights for the comparison cases would play any 
role, at least for ATT.

If you are actually analyzing the matched data using something like a 
ranksum test, I'm not sure how I'd go about using the weights.  I would 
use the weight for the treatment case, at least for ATT (since the 
weight for the two cases wouldn't necessarily be the same one).  But I'm 
not sure what I would do.  (I've started doing analyses on a pair basis 
b/c it lends itself to the types of sensitivity analyses in the 
Rosenbaum book.  But I've not thought through what to do with the 
weights in that case.)
 
I'd be interested in hearing what others would do--
michael

messages.subject: Re: which Stata weight to use?
messages.body_plain:
You want to use frequency or probability weights [depending on whether you 
focus on the insample or population quantity, respectively]. In the 
terminology of our PA article, you want those two empirical distributions 
to be the same. In the case of full matching, you need to weight each 
observation appropriately (using the weights that come out of MatchIt) in 
order to get any benefit of matching.

Kosuke

messages.body_plain:

weights since each obs actually does not appear more than once in your 
sample.

Kosuke
